newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault, Belgian unions far apart after meeting.
newsitem.headline: Renault, Belgian unions far apart after meeting.

text.p: Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer told Belgian union leaders seeking to save the Vilvoorde car plant in Belgium that the decision to close it down was irrevocable.

"I confirmed that this decision was irrevocable," Schweitzer, flanked by security guards, told reporters after a two and a half hour meeting with union representatives in the northern town of Beauvais.

Union leaders said they were disappointed that the company was cold to their proposals on ways to keep the plant open and save 3,100 jobs. They vowed to step up pressure on Renault, which is expected on Thursday to announce huge losses for 1996.
Industry analysts estimate the carmaker will show a loss of between 4.5 and six billion francs ($1.1 billion), its first annual loss in 10 years.
Renault will also face French union calls for protests on Thursday against the company's cost-cutting measures, which include 2,764 job cuts in France this year.

Anni Kerkhove, one of the 11 union representatives who spoke with Schweitzer in Beauvais, told reporters there would be "surprise actions" in France on Thursday. "There will be strikes and work stoppages to disrupt production," she said.

Union leader Vermeersch Hendrik said there was little give-and-take at the meeting. "He was like a recording," Hendrik said of Schweitzer. "He repeated everything he's already said. We'll have to keep up the pressure. We're certain it's already pretty intense," he added.
The union representatives said they got the impression that the company may be flexible on the timetable. Renault has said it wants the plant closed by July 27.

It says the closure is essential to streamlining its car assembly operations in Europe. The car division has been losing money for nearly two years. Schweitzer said Renault's operations were too dispersed among plants that are much smaller and costlier to run than those of its rivals.
The company's performance deteriorated last year, when a downturn in the U.S. and European truck industries drove its commercial vehicle business into the red as well.
Renault's decision to close the plant has triggered outrage across Europe but particularly in Belgium where trade unions denounced the shock announcement as "unbelievably brutal."

Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene on Tuesday urged Schweitzer to consider the unions' proposals. He said they want to keep the plant open, after a restructuring, for two to three years during which a final solution could be worked out.

Schweitzer and the 11 union officials agreed to Wednesday's meeting on "neutral ground" in Beauvais, a northern French city roughly midway between Renault's Paris headquarters and the plant at Vilvoorde in the suburbs of Brussels.

Security was tight after a spate of kidnappings in France by angry workers. The main roads into Beauvais were barred, and riot police surrounded the chamber of commerce building where the meeting was held.
In a brief statement after the meeting, Schweitzer said the company was willing to hold more talks to discuss measures, including internal transfers, to ease the hardship of the closure.
Union leaders want Schweitzer to keep the plant open until it finds a buyer. ($ = 5.65 French Francs)
